assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned the Hubbard model and related many-body problems into controllable, tunable laboratory systems. The Mott-insulator transition, single-site-resolved microscopy and quantum gas microscopes show statistical mechanics of interacting systems directly. Clean model, direct contact with experiment, broad reach across condensed matter, quantum information and statistical physics.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and colleagues) supplied the theoretical proposal; Greiner and Bloch carried out the decisive Mott-insulator and microscopy experiments. Dalibard and Cirac are also credited and could substitute, so the three-person cap forces a real choice. My choice of three is a judgement, not settled history.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of independent confirmation by many groups, and the platform is now routine. Recognition is timely, arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Which of five credited names to leave out is contestable; Jaksch is not on the list.
Overlap with the trapped-ion and Rydberg candidates could split the credit.
I rely on memory for the detailed priority history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fluctuation theorems and Jarzynski equality give exact, universal statements about non-equilibrium work and entropy production, linking microscopic reversibility to the second law. Stochastic thermodynamics is a clean, rigorous framework that is also verified in small systems (colloids, single molecules). This is the kind of simple, general mechanism I value.
assessment.attribution: Evans, Cohen and Morriss (fluctuation theorem), Jarzynski (equality) and Crooks (detailed-balance relation) are the foundational names; Seifert built the stochastic-thermodynamics framework. Four names are credited, so one has to be left out. I would favour Evans, Jarzynski and Seifert, but Crooks's contribution is hard to rank below the others.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed on RNA unfolding, colloidal systems and electronic devices over about two decades. The theory is stable and widely used in biophysics and nanoscale engines.
uncertainties: Credit split between Evans/Cohen/Morriss, Jarzynski, Crooks and Seifert is unresolved, and Cohen and Morriss are not credited here.
Prize committees may see this as less of a discovery of a new phenomenon than a theoretical framework.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Z2 topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect opened a whole field of symmetry-protected topological matter, with a clean theoretical prediction followed by a decisive experiment in HgTe. Impact on condensed matter, materials and quantum information is broad and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the original prediction; Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang's HgTe proposal and Molenkamp's measurement then confirmed it. Zhang is not credited here (and is deceased), and the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is a reasonable configuration. Fu, Moore, Balents and others also contributed to the 3D case.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many groups across 2D and 3D systems, with ARPES and transport; some early materials issues remain, but the concept is solid. Timely, as topology was recognised in 2016 and the next step has not been taken.
uncertainties: The 3D topological insulator contribution (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Hasan) is not covered by these names.
Possible overlap with the quantum anomalous Hall candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The KTHNY theory of defect-mediated two-dimensional melting and the hexatic phase is a classic example of a universal mechanism, built on topological defects and the renormalisation group. It extended the 2016 Kosterlitz-Thouless-type physics, and was confirmed by simulations and colloidal and other experiments.
assessment.attribution: Halperin and Nelson, and Young, developed the two-step melting theory building on Kosterlitz and Thouless. Credit is reasonably clear for Halperin and Nelson; Young's role is smaller but is supplied in the credit set. A Nobel here would need to say clearly that it builds on the earlier prize.
assessment.maturity: Foundational from the late 1970s, with decades of simulation and colloid experiments; some details (first-order versus continuous melting) still depend on the system. Mature, but arguably less urgent now that the central idea was recognised in 2016.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would consider this a distinct enough discovery from the earlier Kosterlitz-Thouless prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Vicsek model and the Toner-Tu hydrodynamic theory established that flocks have true long-range order in two dimensions, in sharp contrast to equilibrium (Mermin-Wagner). A minimal model produced a universal non-equilibrium phase transition, and the field of active matter grew out of it. Strong fit to statistical physics and to my own interests.
assessment.attribution: Vicsek introduced the model and the order-disorder transition; Toner and Tu built the continuum theory that gave the exponents and the breaking of the Mermin-Wagner theorem. Clear, well-defined three-person configuration. Ramaswamy and others contributed to the broader active-matter field.
assessment.maturity: Theory is well established, and experiments with bird flocks, colloidal rollers and bacteria support the picture, though exact exponents are not always confirmed experimentally. Probably somewhat early for a Nobel, but strong.
uncertainties: Quantitative experimental tests of Toner-Tu exponents are limited.
Credit relative to Ramaswamy, Marchetti and the wider active-matter community.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The energy-landscape and funnel picture explains how proteins fold quickly despite an astronomical number of conformations, drawing on spin-glass statistical mechanics. It is a conceptual framework that unified many observations in biophysics.
assessment.attribution: Bryngelson and Wolynes introduced the spin-glass-based principle of minimal frustration; Onuchic and Dill developed and popularised the funnel picture and lattice models. Bryngelson is not credited. The trio is plausible but the individual contributions are intertwined.
assessment.maturity: Widely accepted as a conceptual framework, but it is less a single sharp prediction than an organising principle; AlphaFold's 2024 chemistry prize has altered the context.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would regard this as physics or chemistry, given the 2024 chemistry prize.
Missing co-author Bryngelson in the credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene combines a clean theoretical prediction of flat bands with the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity, creating the field of moire quantum materials. The simplicity of the model and the tunability make it attractive.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated insulator and superconductivity. Dean, Young and others also contributed to related moire phases. A prediction plus experiment pair is a natural configuration.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups, but the origin of the superconductivity is still debated and the field is still moving quickly. Possibly premature.
uncertainties: Other groups (Cao, Dean, Yacoby and others) contributed decisive results.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution links foundations of quantum mechanics to practical secure communication, and has been implemented in real networks and satellites. It is a clear, original idea with lasting conceptual influence on quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) and Ekert (E91, entanglement-based) are the usual names. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea also matters, but is not in the list. The trio is a plausible configuration.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally mature and commercially deployed, though practical security issues remain; the 2022 prize on Bell tests already touched on the foundations, so timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Wiesner's priority and the role of Deutsch, Mermin and others.
